title: Two Brothers from Dayton
summary: Wilbur and Orville Wright got hooked on flying when their dad gave them a little rubber-band flying toy. They grew up to run a bicycle shop, figured out how to balance a flying machine by twisting its wings, and tested big gliders on the windy sand dunes of Kitty Hawk. But their 1901 glider flew so badly that Wilbur almost gave up!

sections.heading: A Flying Toy in Cedar Rapids
paragraphs: It is 1878, in the town of Cedar Rapids, Iowa. Bishop Milton Wright comes home from one of his many church journeys with something hidden in his hands. His two youngest sons crowd around. He tosses the object into the air, and instead of falling, it whirs up toward the ceiling, hovers for a moment, and flutters back down. The boys are amazed.

The toy was a small flying model made of paper, bamboo and cork, with two little propellers spun by a twisted rubber band. It was based on a design by the French inventor Alphonse Pénaud, a clever experimenter with model aircraft. Today we might call it a toy helicopter. The brothers called it the bat. They played with it until it broke, and then they built copies of their own. Years later, they said this toy was where their interest in flying began.

The two boys were Wilbur Wright, then 11, and Orville Wright, then 7. Wilbur was born on 16 April 1867 near Millville, Indiana. Orville was born on 19 August 1871 in Dayton, Ohio. They were two of seven children born to Milton Wright and his wife, Susan Catherine Koerner. Their older brothers were Reuchlin and Lorin, and their younger sister was Katharine, who would become one of their closest supporters. Twins named Otis and Ida died as babies.

Their father was a bishop in a church called the Church of the United Brethren in Christ, and his work meant the family moved a lot: twelve times in all, before finally settling in Dayton in 1884. The house had a large library, and the children were encouraged to read widely and to think for themselves. Their mother, Susan, was very good with tools and machines; she could build and fix household things and even toys for her children. Both brothers later said they got their mechanical skill from her.

The Wright family was also unusually close. The Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum notes that the parents taught their children that family bonds were their most dependable support. That closeness gave Wilbur and Orville a quiet confidence. Later, when famous experts said one thing and the brothers' own tests said another, they were willing to trust their own work.

Neither brother ever married. They lived, worked, argued and invented side by side for most of their lives. Wilbur once wrote that from the time they were little children, he and Orville had lived together, played together and worked together, and thought together. That partnership would become one of the most famous in the history of invention.

sections.heading: Hard Years and a Printing Press
paragraphs: Wilbur was a brilliant student with an extraordinary memory, a good athlete and a fine writer and speaker. People who knew him described him as calm and steady. He planned to go to Yale, one of America's top universities. But in the winter of 1885 to 1886, when Wilbur was 18, he was struck in the face by a stick during a game of ice hockey and lost his front teeth. The injury left him with health problems and he became low and withdrawn. He gave up his plans for Yale.

For the next few years, Wilbur stayed mostly at home. His mother was very ill with tuberculosis, a serious lung disease, and Wilbur cared for her until she died in 1889. During these quiet years, which historians sometimes call his lost years, he read almost everything in his father's library: history, science, literature and religion. All that reading turned out not to be lost at all. It trained him to study a problem carefully and to write about it clearly.

Orville was different: more lively, more impulsive and more optimistic, always taking things apart to see how they worked. He became fascinated by printing. As a teenager he built his own printing press, using parts from an old buggy and other scrap, and in 1889 he left high school after his junior year to start a printing business. Wilbur had also missed out on his diploma when the family moved, so neither brother ever received a high school diploma, though both kept studying hard on their own for the rest of their lives.

Wilbur soon joined Orville's business. Together they published a weekly newspaper for their neighbourhood called the West Side News, and later a daily paper. They also printed work for one of Orville's school friends, Paul Laurence Dunbar, who became one of the first African American poets to win national fame. It was a small business, but it taught the brothers how to run a company, how to build and repair machines, and how to work as a team.

The family home at 7 Hawthorn Street in Dayton would become the place where the brothers talked and argued through their flying ideas, often late into the night. According to family stories, they enjoyed arguing so much that they would sometimes switch sides halfway through, each now defending the other's original point.

sections.heading: Bicycle Men
paragraphs: In the early 1890s, America went bicycle crazy. A new design called the safety bicycle, with two wheels of the same size and a chain driving the back wheel, was much easier and safer to ride than the old high-wheeled penny-farthing. Suddenly everyone wanted one. In December 1892, Wilbur and Orville opened a shop in Dayton to sell and repair bicycles. It started as the Wright Cycle Exchange and was soon renamed the Wright Cycle Company.

The shop moved several times along West Third Street and nearby streets as the business grew. Early bicycles sold for about 40 to 100 dollars each, which was a lot of money then. In 1896 the brothers began building their own bicycles by hand. Their more expensive model was called the Van Cleve, after an ancestor of theirs who was one of Dayton's first settlers, and their cheaper model was the St. Clair. From 1897 to 1909 their shop was at 1127 West Third Street. Many years later, in 1937, the car maker Henry Ford had that building taken apart and rebuilt as a museum exhibit at Greenfield Village in Dearborn, Michigan, where you can still visit it.

The bicycle business mattered for flight in three big ways. First, it earned the money that paid for all their experiments; the Wrights never had a government grant or a rich sponsor. Second, it gave them hands-on skill with light, strong structures: thin metal tubes, wire spokes, chains, sprockets and bearings. Third, and perhaps most important, it taught them about balance.

Think about riding a bike. A bicycle standing still falls over. Yet a rider in motion stays upright by making constant tiny corrections, leaning and steering without even thinking about it. The Wrights came to believe a flying machine would be the same. It did not need to be perfectly stable by itself, any more than a bicycle does. What it needed was a skilled rider with good controls who could keep it balanced moment by moment. That idea would shape everything they did.

In the summer of 1896, Orville fell seriously ill with typhoid fever, a dangerous infection. While he lay in bed recovering, the newspapers reported that Otto Lilienthal had died after his glider crashed. Wilbur read about it, and the brothers talked about it. Lilienthal's flights, and his death, sparked their serious interest in the problem of flight. They began to read whatever they could find, though at first there was not much in Dayton.

sections.heading: A Letter to the Smithsonian
paragraphs: By 1899, Wilbur had decided to study flight properly. On 30 May 1899 he sat down and wrote a letter to the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, D.C., the great national museum and research centre that was then led by Samuel Langley. The letter still survives, two handwritten pages now kept by the National Air and Space Museum.

In it, Wilbur explained that he had been interested in mechanical and human flight since he was a boy, and that he believed flight was possible. He wrote that he wanted to read everything already published on the subject, and that he hoped to add his own small contribution to help whoever would eventually succeed. He was polite, modest and serious. He was not claiming to be a genius; he simply wanted to learn.

The Smithsonian replied quickly. It sent several pamphlets, including writings by Langley and by Lilienthal, and a list of recommended books. The museum's own history says the most important recommendations were Octave Chanute's Progress in Flying Machines and a yearly collection of articles called The Aeronautical Annual. The brothers read everything. In Chanute's book they found a summary of almost every serious attempt to fly up to 1894, including Cayley's ideas, the steam machines of Part 4, and the gliders of Lilienthal and Chanute himself.

Reading all this history, the brothers noticed something important. Many experimenters had worked hard on two of the problems of flight: building wings that could lift a machine, and finding engines powerful enough to drive it. But hardly anyone had solved the third problem: how to balance and steer a machine once it was in the air. Lilienthal and Pilcher had both died because their gliders could not be controlled well enough. Wilbur wrote later that the problem of balance was the real difficulty, and that once a machine could be controlled, the rest would follow.

sections.heading: The Secret in a Twisted Box
paragraphs: So how do you keep a flying machine balanced? Wilbur watched birds for clues. He noticed that when a soaring bird such as a buzzard began to tip to one side, it seemed to correct itself by changing the angle of its wingtips: one tip met the air at a slightly steeper angle, the other at a shallower one. The wing with the steeper angle got more lift and rose, and the bird rolled level again. A bird, Wilbur realised, does not balance by swinging its body like Lilienthal. It balances by changing the shape of its wings.

Could a machine do the same? The brothers first thought about building wings that could pivot on shafts and gears, but that would be heavy and complicated. Then, one day in July 1899, Wilbur was in the bicycle shop chatting with a customer and absent-mindedly fiddling with an empty cardboard box, a long, thin box that had held a bicycle inner tube. He squeezed the ends in opposite directions. The top and bottom of the box twisted, one end tilting up and the other tilting down, but the box stayed strong and in one piece.

Wilbur suddenly saw it. Imagine the top and bottom of the box as the two wings of a biplane. If you could twist the whole wing structure like that, the tips on one side would meet the air at a steeper angle while the tips on the other side met it at a shallower angle. One side would rise and the other would sink, and the machine would roll, just like the bird. There was no need for heavy pivots or gears. You could just twist the wings themselves. The brothers called this idea wing warping.

To test it, they built a biplane kite with a wingspan of about 5 feet (1.5 metres). Its structure was based on the strong, wire-braced double-decker that Chanute and Herring had used for their 1896 glider, but with one important change: the brothers left out the diagonal braces between the front and back posts, so the wings could twist. Four strings ran from the wingtips to two sticks held by the person on the ground. Tilting the sticks in opposite directions twisted the wings.

Around the end of July 1899, Wilbur took the kite to a field near Dayton and flew it. The only people watching were a few schoolboys. When he tilted the sticks, the kite rolled to one side or the other, quickly and exactly as he wanted. It was less than three months after his letter to the Smithsonian, and the brothers already had their first big idea working. No photographs of that kite survive, but a reproduction can be seen today. The next step was to build something big enough to carry a person.

sections.heading: Why Kitty Hawk?
paragraphs: A full-size glider needed a special testing ground. The brothers needed strong, steady winds, so that a glider could stay up while moving slowly over the ground. They needed wide open spaces without trees, and soft ground for crash landings. And they wanted privacy, away from crowds and newspaper reporters. Dayton, with its gentle breezes and busy streets, had none of these things.

So in 1900 Wilbur wrote to the United States Weather Bureau in Washington, D.C., which collected wind records from weather stations across the country. He also asked Octave Chanute for advice. Chanute suggested a sandy seacoast, where sea breezes are strong and sand dunes give soft landings. Studying the wind tables, Wilbur noticed a tiny place called Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, a fishing village on the Outer Banks, a long, narrow chain of sandy islands separated from the mainland by wide sounds of water.

He wrote to the Weather Bureau station at Kitty Hawk. The man in charge there, Joseph Dosher, replied that the beach was wide and free of trees, and that the winds were steady. A local man named William Tate, the village postmaster and its best-educated resident, also wrote back with a warm welcome. 'I will take pleasure in doing all I can for your convenience and success and pleasure,' Tate promised. That settled it.

Getting there was an adventure in itself. In early September 1900, Wilbur set off alone by train from Dayton, carrying pieces of the glider and equipment. In Elizabeth City, North Carolina, he found that hardly anyone even knew how to reach Kitty Hawk. He finally hired a local boatman to sail him across Albemarle Sound in a small, leaky fishing boat, which was battered by a storm on the way. The trip took days. Wilbur stayed with the Tate family until Orville arrived a couple of weeks later with more supplies, and the brothers set up a tent camp in the sand.

Life in camp was rough. The wind blew sand into everything, including their food and their beds. Fresh supplies had to come by boat. In later years, swarms of mosquitoes made some nights almost unbearable. But the brothers loved it too. They wrote cheerful letters home to their sister Katharine about the fish, the wild birds, and the sound of the sea. And the wind, which is what they had come for, blew strong and steady off the ocean.

sections.heading: The 1900 Glider: Flying It Like a Kite
paragraphs: The brothers' first full-size glider, built starting in August 1900, was a biplane with wings spanning about 17.5 feet (about 5.3 metres). It weighed about 52 pounds (about 24 kilograms). It used the same wire-braced structure and wing-warping system they had tested with their kite. But they also made some bold choices that were different from Lilienthal's.

First, the pilot did not hang underneath. He lay flat on his stomach in a gap in the middle of the lower wing. This cut down drag, the air resistance that slows a flying machine, because a person lying down pushes against much less air than one dangling upright. Second, instead of a tail, the glider had a small horizontal surface sticking out in front, called a forward elevator, which the pilot moved with a lever to tilt the nose up or down. The brothers believed this front elevator would help protect them from the kind of sudden nosedive that had killed Lilienthal. Third, the pilot controlled the wing warping with his feet, using a crossbar that twisted the wings.

Most of the time, they flew the 1900 glider as a kite, with ropes held by people on the ground, sometimes with chains or sandbags on board instead of a pilot. This was a clever and safe way to test it. By measuring the pull on the ropes and the angle of the kite, they could work out how much lift and drag the wings made. William Tate's young nephew, Tom Tate, sometimes rode on the glider while it was flown as a tethered kite.

The results were mixed. The glider made less lift than the brothers had calculated, using the standard numbers of the day, so it needed stronger winds than expected to carry a person. But the controls, the museum says, worked beautifully. Near the end of their stay, they took the glider to the big sand dunes called Kill Devil Hills, about 4 miles (6.4 kilometres) south of the village. On 20 October 1900, Wilbur made about a dozen real free glides, sliding down the slope with nobody holding the ropes. In all that first season, their free gliding added up to only about two minutes. But it was enough to show that their ideas about control were sound. They left the glider behind and went home to Dayton, already planning a bigger one.

sections.heading: 1901: The Disappointing Giant
paragraphs: In July 1901 the brothers returned, this time setting up camp right at Kill Devil Hills, closer to the big dunes. They built a wooden shed to hold their new glider and lived in a tent beside it. They had made the 1901 glider much bigger to get more lift: its wings spanned about 22 feet (about 6.7 metres) and it weighed about 98 pounds (about 44 kilograms). It was the largest glider anyone had ever tried to fly. They also made the wings more strongly curved, because the old tables suggested a deeper curve would give more lift.

They had visitors that summer. Octave Chanute came to watch, as he would each year from 1901 to 1903, along with two other experimenters he had introduced to the brothers. The Wrights made many more glides than in 1900, and some were much longer. The giant glider really could carry a person through the air. But almost everything else was a disappointment.

The biggest problem was lift. When the brothers measured it carefully, the 1901 glider was making only about one-third of the lift their calculations had predicted. It is as if you built a bridge expecting it to hold 30 tonnes and found it could hold only 10. Something in the numbers had to be wrong.

There were control problems too. The front elevator became oversensitive and twitchy, so the glider swooped up and down. The brothers flattened the wing curve a little by adjusting the wires, which brought back good pitch control, but lift stayed poor. Stranger still, when the pilot warped the wings to roll into a turn, the glider would sometimes start to turn the right way and then suddenly swing around in the opposite direction. The wing that was lifted more was also being dragged backward more. Engineers now call this adverse yaw. On one hard landing, Wilbur was thrown forward and bruised, though not badly hurt.

The brothers packed up and headed home in August, earlier than they had planned. On the train back to Dayton, Wilbur was gloomier than he had ever been. He reportedly told Orville that men would not fly in their lifetime, and one later version of the story says he said not for a thousand years. These words were remembered and repeated long afterwards, so nobody knows exactly what he said. Wilbur himself, in a speech in 1908, recalled that he had told Orville in 1901 that man would not fly for fifty years. Either way, he was close to giving up.

sections.heading: Trust Nothing, Test Everything
paragraphs: Wilbur did not stay gloomy for long. Octave Chanute invited him to give a talk in Chicago to the Western Society of Engineers, an important club of professional engineers. Wilbur was nervous, but his sister Katharine urged him to accept. On 18 September 1901 he stood before the audience and gave a careful report on the gliders of 1900 and 1901, illustrated with lantern slides, the projected photographs of the day. It was the first public account of the brothers' experiments. Preparing the talk forced Wilbur to go back over all their measurements, one by one.

As he did, a startling thought grew stronger. Perhaps the problem was not their glider at all. Perhaps the problem was the numbers everybody used. To predict the lift of a wing, experimenters of the day used a formula that included a value for air pressure called the Smeaton coefficient, worked out back in the 1700s, together with tables of measurements such as Lilienthal's famous table for curved wings. The Wrights had trusted these numbers, just as everyone else did. But their 1901 glider was making only a third of the lift those numbers promised. Either the brothers were doing something very wrong, or the most respected data in the field was wrong.

That was a bold thought for two bicycle makers with no college degrees. Lilienthal was the hero they admired most. Chanute was their friend and adviser. Questioning the great experts felt almost rude. But the brothers had grown up in a family that taught them to think for themselves, and they had spent years arguing ideas back and forth until the truth came out.

So, in the autumn of 1901, Wilbur and Orville made a decision that would change the history of flight. They would stop trusting other people's numbers. They would build their own testing equipment, right there in the back of the bicycle shop, and measure the lift of wings themselves, carefully and patiently, one shape at a time. As Part 7 will show, their homemade wind tunnel was about to uncover the secret everyone else had missed.

deepDive: Why did the 1901 glider make only about a third of its predicted lift? The Wrights, like everyone else, estimated lift with an equation of the form lift = k x S x V squared x CL, where S is wing area, V is airspeed, CL is a lift coefficient read from a table (often Lilienthal's), and k is the Smeaton coefficient, a number for the pressure of air, originally from 18th-century work associated with John Smeaton and long given as about 0.005. Part 7 tells how their own experiments showed k was nearer 0.0033, roughly a third lower, which explains much of the shortfall. Historians also point to another issue, noted by the Smithsonian: Lilienthal's table described one specific wing curve and measured angles in a particular way, and applying it to the Wrights' differently shaped, more deeply curved 1901 wings was a mismatch. The brothers measured their own lift by flying the gliders as kites and recording the pull on the lines and the angle of the tether, a clever field method that let them compare reality with prediction. The 1901 season also revealed adverse yaw. When wing warping increases the angle of one wing to raise it, that wing gets more lift but also more drag, so it is pulled backward and the nose swings the wrong way. The Wrights did not fully solve this until 1902, when they added a movable rudder linked to the warping (Part 7). Their choice of a forward elevator, or canard, is debated too. It gave them a visible, responsive pitch control and they believed it softened stalls, but it made the craft less naturally stable, which suited their bicycle-inspired view that a pilot should actively balance the machine. Later designers mostly moved the elevator to the tail. Finally, the famous gloomy quotation deserves care. Wilbur's remark on the train was recalled years later, and versions differ: 'not in our lifetime', 'not within a thousand years', or, in Wilbur's own 1908 recollection, 'not for fifty years'. What is certain is the result: instead of quitting, the brothers decided to test the data themselves.
funFact: The Wright brothers' idea for steering an airplane, wing warping, came to Wilbur while he was idly twisting an empty bicycle inner-tube box in their bicycle shop.
